what_its_for: Ibalizumab-uiyk is used to treat HIV-1 infection in adults who have already tried many other HIV medicines that no longer work well for them. It is always used together with other HIV medicines. It does not cure HIV, but it helps lower the amount of virus in your body and helps keep your immune system stronger.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as an IV infusion (a slow injection into your vein) by a healthcare provider in a clinic or infusion center. You will not give this medicine to yourself at home. Each infusion takes about 15 to 30 minutes. You will be watched by medical staff during and after the infusion to make sure you are feeling okay.
dosing: Your first dose is a one-time loading dose of 2,000 mg given into your vein. After that, you will receive a maintenance dose of 800 mg every 2 weeks. Your doctor will schedule your regular appointments to keep you on track. Always keep your infusion appointments so your HIV stays under control.
missed_dose: It is very important to keep all of your scheduled infusion appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or infusion center right away. If more than 3 days pass after a missed dose, your doctor may need to give you the higher loading dose again before restarting your regular schedule. Do not try to skip or delay doses on your own.
storage: This medicine is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at the clinic or infusion center. You do not need to store it at home. If you are given information about home storage for any reason, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C and 8°C). Do not freeze it. Keep it in the original carton to protect it from light.
what_to_avoid: Do not miss your scheduled infusion appointments, as skipping doses can allow the HIV virus to grow and become harder to treat. Talk to your doctor before starting any new prescription medicines, over-the-counter drugs, vitamins, or herbal supplements, as some may affect how this medicine works. Do not share needles, syringes, or personal items that may carry blood, as HIV can still be passed to others even while you are on treatment.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or get emergency help right away if you have any signs of an infusion reaction such as dizziness, nausea, rash, chills, flushing, sweating, trouble breathing, or chest tightness during or after your infusion. Also call your doctor if you notice signs of infection such as fever, unusual tiredness, or swollen lymph nodes. Tell your doctor right away if you become pregnant or plan to become pregnant.
when_it_works: This medicine starts working right away to block HIV from entering your immune cells. However, it may take several weeks to months to see improvements in your lab results, such as a lower viral load and a higher CD4 cell count. Keep taking all of your HIV medicines as directed even if you feel well, because HIV can still be active even when you have no symptoms.
special_populations: This medicine has not been well studied in children, so it is currently only approved for adults 18 years and older. If you are pregnant or breastfeeding, talk to your doctor before using this medicine. HIV-positive mothers are generally advised not to breastfeed to avoid passing the virus to their baby. There is no specific dose adjustment needed for older adults or people with kidney or liver problems, but always keep your doctor informed about all of your health conditions.
